item.title: 2 baby meerkats make their debut at Peruvian zoo, spotlighting conservation
item.description:
2 baby meerkats make their debut at Peruvian zoo, spotlighting conservation
A private zoo in Peru has introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima to raise awareness about wildlife conservationByMAURICIO MUÑOZ Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 4:00 PM
Share
LIMA, Peru -- A private zoo in Peru on Wednesday introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima as part of an effort to raise awareness about wildlife conservation and introduce visitors to the African species.
Eduardo Espíritu, a biologist in charge of mammals at NaviFauna, a private zoo and wildlife refuge, said the initiative aims to educate the public about the importance of protecting biodiversity.
Meerkats are small mammals native to southern Africa that dig underground burrows and often stand upright to keep watch for potential threats.
“Meerkats cannot be pets. They are wild animals,” Espíritu said. “We focus on keeping them healthy, and one sign of that is reproduction,” something the zoo has successfully achieved in Lima.
The zoo is home to 15 meerkats, eight of which have been born in Lima since 2025. The other seven arrived from their native Botswana in 2022 through an exchange between zoos, according to NaviFauna.

item.title: South Africa's Biovac aims to dramatically increase vaccine production with help from an EU loan
item.description:
South Africa's Biovac aims to dramatically increase vaccine production with help from an EU loan
South African pharmaceutical company Biovac says it aims to dramatically increase its vaccine production by the end of 2028 with help from a 75-million euro loan from the European Union's investment bankByGERALD IMRAY Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 2:54 PM
Share
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- South Africa’s Biovac said Wednesday that a new manufacturing facility aims to dramatically increase African production of vaccines by the end of 2028 to help reduce the continent’s heavy reliance on imported doses.
Africa needs more than 1 billion vaccine doses a year, but only around 1% of them are manufactured on the continent, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Biovac, a public-private pharmaceutical company that's part-owned by the South African government, distributes or does end-stage production for vaccines for polio, tuberculosis, tetanus and other diseases.
It's also seeking regulatory approval to start end-to-end production of an oral cholera vaccine by late 2028, company officials said.
It would be the first cholera vaccine manufactured entirely in Africa and only the second vaccine produced end-to-end on the continent, following a yellow fever vaccine produced by Senegal's Pasteur Institute.
Biovac acquired the base technology for its cholera vaccine from the International Vaccine Institute in South Korea, Biovac CEO Morena Makhoana said. He added that the vaccine is currently undergoing clinical trials and the company expects to have initial safety and efficacy data by June.
Biovac plans to upscale its overall vaccine production by building a new manufacturing facility next to its current base in Cape Town with support from the European Union's investment bank.

item.title: Fuel tanker crash ignites a massive fire on a highway surrounding Cairo, killing at least 31 people
item.description:
Fuel tanker crash ignites a massive fire on a highway surrounding Cairo, killing at least 31 people
A crash involving a fuel tanker has ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo, killing at least 31 peopleByFAY ABUELGASIM Associated Press and MOHAMMED SALAH Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 2:14 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
CAIRO -- A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.
The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the Health Ministry.
The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighborhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the Health Ministry.
At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.
“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire," he told the AP, describing the fear and panic that followed. "It was a shocking scene.”
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The Public Prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were underway to identify the victims.

item.title: Fighting in eastern Congo forces Ebola workers to evacuate, threatening outbreak response
item.description:
Fighting in eastern Congo forces Ebola workers to evacuate, threatening outbreak response
Escalating fighting in eastern Congo has forced health workers to evacuate and blocked roads needed to reach Ebola patientsByCONSTANT SAME BAGALWA Associated Press and MARK BANCHEREAU Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 1:50 PM
Share
BUNIA, Congo -- Escalating fighting in eastern Congo has forced Ebola response workers to leave affected areas and disrupted efforts to contain the deadliest outbreak in the country, health officials and humanitarian workers said Wednesday.
The fighting between the army and rebel groups has prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, said Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager.
Congo’s Ebola outbreak has infected more than 11,700 people and killed more than 5,700 since it was declared in May, according to the latest government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing it requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.
The clashes between government forces and the Convention for the Popular Revolution, or CRP, have intensified north of Bunia, the capital of the northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.
CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises.

item.title: Nigeria seizes $220 million worth of meth, arrests 5 Mexican suspects in major bust
item.description:
Nigeria seizes $220 million worth of meth, arrests 5 Mexican suspects in major bust
Nigeria’s anti-drug agency says it seized at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrested five Mexican suspects in a major operation in the African country's southeastByDYEPKAZAH SHIBAYAN Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 1:10 PM
Share
ABUJA, Nigeria -- ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — Nigeria’s anti-drug agency on Wednesday announced the seizure of at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and the arrest of five Mexican suspects in a major drug operation in the country's southeast.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said its operatives stormed an industrial-scale laboratory in Enugu state where “Mexican meth specialists” were arrested. The Mexicans were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national before entering the country with forged passports, agency spokesman Femi Babafemi said in a statement.
“A total of 1,512 kilograms of methamphetamine, finished and in production, with an estimated value of $226.8 million was recovered from the clandestine factory," Babafemi said.
It is one of the largest seizures this year in a country that has emerged as a hot spot for illegal drugs. A transnational drug syndicate involving Nigerians and Mexicans was busted in southwestern Nigeria in May, one of several such operations carried out recently.

item.title: Puerto Rico's Supreme Court cancels a key power contract and many wonder what's next
item.description:
Puerto Rico's Supreme Court cancels a key power contract and many wonder what's next
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy, following a contentious legal fight with the private power companyByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 12:48 PM
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a contentious legal fight with the private power company.
The 5-4 ruling of more than 200 pages, made public on Wednesday, plunges the island into further uncertainty as many wonder who will take over from Luma while power outages persist across the U.S. territory and crews continue to repair the grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.
Puerto Rico’s government had sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Gov. Jenniffer González to cancel the contract.
The court awarded one year for officials to figure out their next steps. González said her administration would seek a new company and that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority.
She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions" and “unnecessary outages,” asserting they have enough money to provide proper service as she accused them of lacking diligence and driving the cost of electricity in the U.S. territory to a record high.
“You have seen the substations on fire,” she said. “They have not yet been able to explain why.”
As the governor spoke, a federal control board that oversees the island's finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of service.
“The Puerto Rican government's decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there's no “clear plan or successor company in place.”

item.title: Kenya cult leader found guilty of new assault and cruelty charges
item.description:
Kenya cult leader found guilty of new assault and cruelty charges
Jailed Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie has been found guilty of assault and cruelty to children in a new caseByEVELYNE MUSAMBI Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 12:28 PM
NAIROBI, Kenya -- NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Jailed Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie was on Wednesday found guilty of assault and cruelty to children in a new case, following the deaths of more than 400 people who allegedly starved to death after he told his followers to fast until they met Jesus.
Mackenzie, who was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Nov. 7 over the murder of 190 children and one adult, will now be sentenced for the new charges on Dec. 17.
He was charged at a court in the coastal city of Mombasa alongside 11 of his followers, while 24 other people were acquitted.
Principal Magistrate Nelly Chepchirchir emphasized the need to distinguish the parents’ responsibility from the religious beliefs they held, saying religion wasn't an excuse for subjecting children to cruelty.
The six children cited in the case were allegedly required to fast before their parents so they could meet Jesus first. Those who attempted to escape or secretly eat or drink were tied up, beaten and locked up.
Mackenzie is also facing separate radicalization charges, with a judgment expected on Thursday.

item.title: New Miss Universe's Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win
item.description:
New Miss Universe's Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win
The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose people have long been known as “the cucumbers.”ByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 9:33 AM
Share
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers.”
Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.
“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.
The town of some 39,000 people — named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers — could barely contain itself.
“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.
“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”
Barreto, 27, has one daughter and holds master’s degrees in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the U.S. Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviors.
“Her journey is a powerful reminder that motherhood, marriage and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive, and that a woman’s potential should never be defined by the stage of life she is in,” Ronald Day, CEO of the Miss Universe Organization, said in a statement.
The organization began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023. The pageant has lost favor in some countries, with critics saying it objectifies women and promotes unrealistic body ideals.
Barreto is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island.

item.title: Pope creates new Vatican initiative to coordinate church's prison ministry in sign it's a priority
item.description:
Pope creates new Vatican initiative to coordinate church's prison ministry in sign it's a priority
Pope Leo XIV has launched a new global initiative to coordinate the Catholic Church’s spiritual care for inmatesByThe Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 9:24 AM
Share
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV, who has followed Pope Francis in making prison ministry a priority, created a new global initiative on Wednesday to coordinate the Catholic Church’s spiritual care for inmates.
Leo named the archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge Ignacio García Cuerva, as the first coordinator of the service for prisoners’ pastoral care. The new entity reports to the Vatican’s development and charity office.
Just a few weeks ago, García Cuerva welcomed Leo to the Devoto Prison in Buenos Aires on the last day of the pontiff’s visit to Argentina. Francis had ministered at Devoto for years as archbishop, and went on to schedule prison visits throughout his pontificate during his foreign trips and even while in Rome.
Leo has followed suit, visiting inmates at a notorious prison in Equatorial Guinea and then in Buenos Aires. The message has been to encourage inmates to have hope, and to show they are still beloved children of God. In Buenos Aires, Leo urged the inmates to see their time behind bars as a chance for redemption and reconciliation.
Prison ministry is an important tenet of the Catholic faith, following the Biblical mandate “I was in prison, and you came to me.”

item.title: UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
item.description:
UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their childrenByDANICA KIRKA Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 7:06 AM
LONDON -- Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children.
Andy Burnham made the announcement Tuesday night on the BBC’s Newsnight program, saying the panel’s chairman would be “relentless in his pursuit of the facts.” An estimated 22,000 British military personnel witnessed Cold War-era nuclear weapons tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans from 1952 to 1967.
“Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish,” Burnham said in a statement.
Veterans claim Britain’s Ministry of Defense intentionally hid data from blood and urine samples that would demonstrate how they were unwittingly used as test subjects to investigate the impact of nuclear explosions on humans.
Former Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood said in September that he had “inadvertently misled” Parliament in 2018 when he told lawmakers the Ministry of Defense had been unable to locate any information about such blood testing. He later learned that blood samples were taken throughout the military, although veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses related to radiation exposure were unable to access them.
“This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed,” Ellwood wrote in the Guardian.
